name: Kaal Corpus claim status overlay
author: Wulf A. Kaal
note: Hand-maintained supersession and decay record for the claim layer. This file is the source of truth for claim status and is NOT regenerated by the extraction pipeline. tools/overlay.py merges confirmed entries into the published artifacts after every rebuild. review_state must be 'confirmed' before an entry reaches the public JSON; 'proposed' entries are drafts awaiting the author's sign-off.

status.superseded: A later work by the author replaces this claim. superseded_by is required.
status.falsified: External evidence contradicts the claim. evidence is required.
status.narrowed: The claim holds only under conditions narrower than those originally stated. See revised_scope.

review_state.proposed: Drafted by a research-loop cycle. Not published.
review_state.confirmed: Reviewed and endorsed by the author. Published.
review_state.rejected: Reviewed and declined. Retained for the record; never published.

kaal:claim:3782201-012.reason: The claim holds that neural networks are 'always extremely unreliable when applied to novel situations.' Frontier model performance on held-out and adversarially novel tasks between 2023 and 2026 contradicts the unqualified form of this claim. The underlying institutional argument may survive; the empirical premise as stated does not.

kaal:claim:3071378-035.reason: The claim that dilution by central administrators is 'impossible' because token supply is predetermined in code holds only where supply is genuinely fixed and no mint authority or upgradeable proxy exists. Observed DAO practice 2017-2026 includes governance-authorised minting, treasury issuance, and upgradeable contracts, all of which reintroduce dilution.
revised_scope: fixed-supply tokens with no mint function

kaal:claim:3071378-037.reason: The claim that reputational penalties in a DAO are 'entirely free from racial implications because token holders are unlikely to even know each other' assumes durable pseudonymity. Doxxing, off-chain coordination in Discord and Telegram, on-chain clustering analysis, and named delegate systems have made DAO participation substantially identified since 2017.
